analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to pay workers a dividend matching stock-buyback spending and tightens buyback rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2019 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one hearing in November 2020, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require publicly traded companies that buy back their own stock to pay their non-executive workers a cash amount based on what the company spent on buybacks and on increased or special dividends. It would also make buyback plans more transparent by requiring companies to tell the Securities and Exchange Commission why they are buying back stock, cap the share of daily trading volume a company can buy, and bar executives from selling their own shares for a week after a buyback is announced.
analysis.who_benefits: Non-executive workers at large public companies — including temps, contractors, staffing-agency workers, and franchise workers — would receive a cash payment scaled to hours worked, and would gain the right to sue and collect attorney's fees if the company fails to pay.

how_it_helps.text: Each year a covered company spends money repurchasing its own stock, or increases or pays special dividends, it must divide that total among its eligible workers, with the share rising from 25% to 100% based on hours worked during the year.

The bill repeals the SEC rule (Rule 10b-18) that currently shields buybacks from manipulation claims, and instead makes buybacks unlawful unless the company discloses its rationale, the size of the plan, the source of funds, and weekly purchase details.

It caps daily repurchases at 15% of a stock's average daily trading volume — tighter than the current 25% rule it replaces — and bars executive officers from selling company shares for seven days after a buyback announcement.

Workers who are shortchanged can sue in federal or state court for the payment plus liquidated damages and attorney's fees, and mandatory arbitration agreements cannot block that claim; the bill also prohibits companies from retaliating against workers because they are eligible for a payment.

analysis.who_pays: The companies and their shareholders: money that would have gone to buybacks and dividend increases is redirected to worker payments, and companies face new disclosure, trading, and enforcement costs.

drawbacks.text: A company can avoid owing any worker dividend simply by not buying back stock and keeping ordinary dividends flat, since the payment is calculated only from buyback spending, dividend increases, and special dividends — so the mechanism works through market behavior rather than a guaranteed payment.

Restricting how and when companies repurchase shares reduces a tool firms use to return cash to shareholders, which critics note also includes the retirement accounts and mutual funds that ordinary savers hold; the bill's own findings acknowledge that buybacks compete with capital spending and research and development for company cash.

The bill's reach extends beyond direct employees to contractors, staffing-agency workers, and franchise workers, which multiplies the recordkeeping and payment obligations for covered companies and their private-sector counterparties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a deliberate transfer of corporate cash from shareholders to workers, and on its own terms it would work: the bill includes enforcement, private lawsuits, anti-retaliation protection, and an override of forced arbitration. The main honest limitation is that it pays nothing unless a company actually buys back stock or raises dividends, so the benefit to workers rises and falls with shareholder-friendly capital returns rather than with company profitability or worker productivity.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee for the rest of the Congress; the committee held one hearing but never voted on it, and no floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 31, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No senator joined as a cosponsor.
On November 17, 2020, the Banking Committee held hearings on the bill (printed as S.Hrg. 116-456), but the committee took no further action and the bill never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large public companies and their executives and major shareholders, who kept buying back stock under the existing rules with no worker-share requirement; workers at those companies received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public companies, executives, and major shareholders

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; as the bill's author he was the only senator publicly attached to it.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred; the bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and died in a Republican-chaired committee without a markup.

industries.industry: Large public corporations and their executives and major shareholders
industries.note: Buyback spending would effectively be shared with workers, buyback plans would face tighter disclosure and trading limits, and executives could not sell shares for a week after announcing a buyback. The bill's findings note S&P 500 companies spent $806 billion on buybacks in 2018 alone.

The bill restricts buyback execution to one broker per day, limits purchase timing, caps daily volume at 15% of average trading volume, and requires weekly filings identifying the executing broker-dealer, reducing the volume and flexibility of a business line that serves buyback programs.

Tighter buyback rules could slow the share-price support buybacks provide to mutual funds and 401(k) holdings, though worker payments would partly offset that by putting more cash in the hands of consumers.
